activities.title: Check the date
activities.officeDescription: Check which year a growth figure describes.
activities.intro: The headline says “this year.” Check the report before you share it.
activities.sourceIntro: Compare the report’s year with the date on the headline.
activities.sourceExplanation: Users rose from 100,000 in 2024 to 180,000 in 2025. That is 80% growth in 2025. The report was published in February 2026.
activities.challengeTitle: The year needs to be clear.
activities.challengeText: The headline is dated September 2026, but the report measures growth from 2024 to 2025. It does not show how user numbers changed in 2026.
activities.correctedFeedback: You checked the report again and added 2025. The headline now matches the source.
activities.successFeedback: You added 2025. The headline now matches the year in the report.
activities.journalEvidence: The report compared 100,000 users in 2024 with 180,000 in 2025. The headline was dated September 2026, so “this year” did not match the figures.

choices.label: Add the year
choices.detail: In 2025, users grew 80%.

activities.title: Sales and profit
activities.officeDescription: See why higher sales can still mean lower profit.
activities.intro: Sales increased. Check the costs before deciding what happened to profit.
activities.sourceIntro: Sales are money from selling. Profit is what remains after costs.
activities.sourceExplanation: All amounts are dollars. In this simplified example, profit equals sales minus the costs shown.
activities.draftHeadline: Sales rose by 50%, so profit rose too.
activities.correctedHeadline: Sales rose by 50%, but profit fell by 50%.
activities.challengeTitle: Higher sales do not always mean higher profit.
activities.challengeText: Sales rose from $1,000 to $1,500. Costs rose from $600 to $1,300. After costs, profit fell from $400 to $200. Compare both before making the claim.
activities.correctedFeedback: You checked the costs and corrected the headline. Profit fell even though sales increased.
activities.successFeedback: You checked sales and costs. Sales increased, but the company kept less money as profit.
activities.journalEvidence: In 2024, sales were $1,000 and costs were $600, leaving $400 profit. In 2025, sales were $1,500 and costs were $1,300, leaving $200 profit. Costs grew more than sales, so profit fell.

choices.label: Check costs
choices.detail: Costs rose faster. Profit fell from $400 to $200.

choices.label: Use sales alone
choices.detail: Sales rose by 50%, so profit must have risen too.

activities.title: Compare company value
activities.officeDescription: Look beyond the price of one share.
activities.intro: The team called Harbor the smaller company because one share costs less. Check the whole company.
activities.sourceIntro: Use both the price and the number of shares.
activities.sourceExplanation: A lower share price does not establish a lower total stock-market value.
activities.draftHeadline: Harbor is smaller because its shares cost $5.
activities.correctedHeadline: Harbor’s total stock-market value is $2,000; Aster’s is $1,000.
activities.challengeTitle: One share is only a piece.
activities.challengeText: Harbor has four times as many shares outstanding. Multiply each price by its share count. The resulting market value is not a measure of whether an investment is good value.
activities.correctedFeedback: You included the share counts. Harbor has the larger total stock-market value in this example.
activities.successFeedback: You checked the price and the share count together. A cheaper single share can belong to a company with a larger market value.
activities.journalEvidence: At the same moment, Aster had 100 shares at $10 each, or $1,000 in total. Harbor had 400 shares at $5 each, or $2,000. This comparison does not establish which company is a better investment.

choices.label: Compare one share
choices.detail: $5 is less than $10, so Harbor must have the smaller total value.

evidence.title: Two fictional companies · same moment
evidence.explanation: Each company has one share class in this example. Multiply the share price by all outstanding shares to compare their total stock-market values. This does not tell us which is a better investment.

activities.title: Count the fees
activities.officeDescription: Separate the amount spent from the amount invested.
activities.intro: This estimate says ten dollars spent means ten dollars in shares. Follow where the money goes.
activities.sourceIntro: The purchase fee is included in the total budget.
activities.sourceExplanation: Spending and investment value are different amounts when fees are charged.
activities.draftHeadline: I spent $10, so my shares are worth $10.
activities.correctedHeadline: The $10 budget covers a $1 fee and $9 in shares.
activities.challengeTitle: The fee does not buy a share.
activities.challengeText: Subtract the $1 purchase fee from the $10 budget. That leaves $9, buying three $3 shares. With the share price unchanged, their value is $9 before any future selling costs.
activities.correctedFeedback: You separated the fee from the shares. The saved estimate now accounts for the whole budget.
activities.successFeedback: You followed all ten dollars: one for the fee and nine for the shares. The amount spent is not the starting value of the holding.
activities.journalEvidence: The fictional estimate has a $10 total budget, a $1 purchase fee and a $3 share price. It buys 3 shares worth $9 at that price. No price movement, spread, tax or other purchase costs are assumed; future selling costs are excluded.

choices.label: $9 in shares
choices.detail: $1 pays the fee. The remaining $9 buys 3 shares at $3 each.

choices.label: $10 in shares
choices.detail: All $10 spent counts as the value of the shares.

evidence.title: Fictional order estimate · US dollars
evidence.explanation: The fee comes out of the budget. Assume no spread, tax, price movement or other purchase charges. Future selling costs are not included. This is an exercise, not an executable quote.

activities.title: Check concentration
activities.officeDescription: Count the companies behind the purchases.
activities.intro: Three purchases look like three separate risks. Check which companies are behind them.
activities.sourceIntro: Group the two Aster purchases before calculating their share of the total.
activities.sourceExplanation: Separate purchases can still depend on the same company.
activities.draftHeadline: Three purchases spread the money equally across three companies.
activities.correctedHeadline: 80% of these holdings is in Aster; 20% is in Harbor.
activities.challengeText: Both the $60 January purchase and the $20 June purchase depend on Aster. Together they make up $80 of $100, or 80%. The remaining $20 is in Harbor. A count of purchase lines does not measure diversification.
activities.correctedFeedback: You grouped the purchases by company. The notes now show how much depends on Aster.
activities.successFeedback: You looked through the purchase dates and found the shared company. Most of this example depends on Aster.
activities.journalEvidence: The current values are $60 in the January Aster purchase, $20 in the June Aster purchase and $20 in Harbor. Aster accounts for $80 ÷ $100 = 80%. These are two companies, and diversification does not eliminate the risk of loss.

choices.label: 80% is in Aster
choices.detail: The two Aster purchases total $80 of the $100 holdings.

choices.label: Three equal company risks
choices.detail: Each purchase is a separate line, so there are three equally weighted companies.

evidence.title: Fictional holdings · current values
evidence.explanation: The two Aster purchases are shares in the same company. Group holdings by the company they depend on, even when they were bought at different times. Diversification cannot guarantee against losses.

activities.title: Prepare the comparison
activities.officeDescription: Bring company value, fees and concentration into one clear note.
activities.intro: The team wants a comparison, not a guess about which stock will win. Check your three sources and choose the note they support.
activities.sourceIntro: These are three separate practice examples. Keep each conclusion tied to its own figures.
activities.sourceExplanation: Company value, an order estimate and a set of holdings answer different questions.
activities.draftHeadline: What can we say from these three examples?
activities.correctedHeadline: Harbor has the larger total stock-market value. The $10 order puts $9 into shares. The practice holdings are 80% Aster.
activities.challengeTitle: Give each source its own conclusion.
activities.challengeText: Harbor’s total stock-market value is $5 × 400 = $2,000. In the order example, the fee leaves $9 for shares. In the holdings example, $80 of $100 depends on Aster. None of these facts predicts a winner.
activities.correctedFeedback: You revised the comparison and kept each conclusion within its evidence. Both your first answer and the corrected note are saved.
activities.successFeedback: You checked the whole company, followed the fee and grouped the holdings. Your comparison gives the team facts without promising an outcome.
activities.journalEvidence: The separate examples establish three facts: Harbor’s total stock-market value is $2,000 versus Aster’s $1,000; the $10 order buys $9 in shares after its $1 fee; and 80% of the $100 practice holdings is in Aster. The sources do not establish future returns or which investment is better.

choices.label: Keep all three checks
choices.detail: Harbor’s total is $2,000. The order buys $9 in shares. The separate holdings are 80% Aster. These facts do not pick a winner.

choices.label: Choose the cheapest share
choices.detail: Harbor’s lower share price proves it is the better investment; the other checks can wait.

choices.label: Leave out the fee
choices.detail: Harbor’s total is $2,000 and the holdings are 80% Aster. The order puts the full $10 into shares.

evidence.title: Two fictional companies · same moment
evidence.explanation: Each company has one share class in this example. Multiply the share price by all outstanding shares to compare their total stock-market values. This does not tell us which is a better investment.

evidence.title: Fictional order estimate · US dollars
evidence.explanation: The fee comes out of the budget. Assume no spread, tax, price movement or other purchase charges. Future selling costs are not included. This is an exercise, not an executable quote.

evidence.title: Fictional holdings · current values
evidence.explanation: The two Aster purchases are shares in the same company. Group holdings by the company they depend on, even when they were bought at different times. Diversification cannot guarantee against losses.

activities.title: Review the team’s update
activities.officeDescription: Nia has a sales update with one important figure missing.
activities.intro: Nia from the research team has brought a new Aster sales note. Decide what the team can responsibly do while its costs are missing.
activities.sourceIntro: The sales comparison is complete. The current cost figure is not in the note, so profit cannot be compared yet.
activities.sourceExplanation: This is a fictional internal update. Both choices keep the missing costs explicit and avoid an unsupported profit claim.
activities.draftHeadline: Sales rose by 50%. What should the team do next?
activities.correctedHeadline: State only the sales result, or wait for costs before comparing profit.
activities.challengeText: A sales-only update must say that costs are missing. A profit comparison must wait for those costs. Either responsible action can move the work forward.
activities.correctedFeedback: You kept the missing costs visible before committing the team’s next step.
activities.successFeedback: Your decision is saved. Nia can now respond to the exact action you chose.
activities.journalEvidence: Current sales were $1,500 versus $1,000 previously, a 50% increase. Current costs were absent, so the note did not support a profit claim.

choices.label: Share a qualified update
choices.detail: Sales rose 50%. Costs are missing, so this update makes no claim about profit.

choices.label: Request the missing costs
choices.detail: Ask Nia for the current costs before the team makes any comparison about profit.

evidence.title: Nia’s sales note
evidence.explanation: Sales rose by 50%. Without current costs, this note cannot establish whether profit rose or fell.

request-missing-costs.officeConsequence: Nia: I have your request for the missing costs. I’ll return with the figures before we compare profit.

activities.correctedHeadline: Sales rose by 50%, while profit fell from $400 to $200.
activities.challengeTitle: The returned costs change what can be concluded.
activities.challengeText: Current costs were $1,300. Subtracting them from $1,500 sales leaves $200 profit, down from the previous $400.
activities.correctedFeedback: You used the returned costs. The comparison now separates sales growth from profit decline.
activities.successFeedback: You checked Nia’s returned figures. The team can now revisit the earlier action with a supported profit comparison.
activities.journalEvidence: Previous profit was $1,000 − $600 = $400. Current profit was $1,500 − $1,300 = $200. Sales rose by 50%, while profit fell by 50%.

activities.title: Set a loss limit
activities.officeDescription: Decide how much of a budget you could invest and still be fine.
activities.intro: The draft plan puts a whole month’s money into one stock. Check what that money is already needed for.
activities.sourceIntro: Only the spare amount is money you could lose without changing your month.
activities.sourceExplanation: Rent, food and savings are already spoken for. The spare amount is what is left after them. These are invented figures for practice.
activities.draftHeadline: Put the whole $200 into one stock this month.
activities.correctedHeadline: Invest only the $20 spare and leave rent, food and savings alone.
activities.challengeTitle: Only spare money can go at risk.
activities.challengeText: Rent, food and savings take $180 of the $200, leaving $20 spare. A stock can fall to nothing, so only money you could lose without harm should go in. This is a fictional exercise, not advice about your own money.
activities.correctedFeedback: You kept the committed money safe and set the $20 spare as the limit. The plan now risks only what could be lost.
activities.successFeedback: You invested only the $20 spare. Rent, food and savings stay untouched, whatever the stock does.
activities.journalEvidence: In this fictional budget, $200 for the month covered $120 rent, $50 food and $10 savings, leaving $20 spare. Only that $20 was set as money that could be lost. Prices can fall, and this exercise is not advice about real money.

choices.label: Invest the spare only
choices.detail: Keep rent, food and savings. Invest the $20 you could lose without harm.

choices.label: Invest everything
choices.detail: Put all $200 in, and find another way to cover rent and food.

evidence.title: Fictional monthly budget · US dollars
evidence.explanation: Rent, food and savings are already committed. Only the spare amount could be lost without changing the month. These figures are invented for practice, not advice about your own money.

activities.title: A plan is not a promise
activities.officeDescription: Tell a plan you can keep from a return no one can promise.
activities.intro: The draft promises what the money will become. Check what a plan can actually control.
activities.sourceIntro: A plan lists actions and limits you choose. It cannot set the price.
activities.sourceTitle: A plan you can keep, and a promise you cannot
activities.sourceExplanation: You control how much to invest, when to review and when to sell. You do not control the price, so the return cannot be promised. These figures are invented for practice.
activities.draftHeadline: This plan will turn the $20 into $30.
activities.correctedHeadline: Invest the $20 spare, review in three months, and accept that the return is not guaranteed.
activities.challengeTitle: A plan sets actions, not outcomes.
activities.challengeText: You can decide how much to invest, when to review and when to sell. You cannot decide the price, so no honest plan promises $30. These are fictional figures for practice.
activities.correctedFeedback: You rewrote the plan as actions and a limit. It no longer promises a return you cannot control.
activities.successFeedback: You kept the plan to what you can decide. A plan guides your actions; it cannot guarantee the result.
activities.journalEvidence: The draft promised the $20 would become $30. The corrected plan set actions and a limit instead: invest the spare, review in three months, sell at $10, with no guaranteed return. These are fictional figures for practice.

choices.label: State actions and a limit
choices.detail: Invest the $20 spare, review in three months, and sell if it drops to $10. Returns are not guaranteed.

choices.label: Promise a return
choices.detail: The plan will grow the $20 into $30 within three months.

evidence.title: A plan you can keep, and a promise you cannot
evidence.explanation: The first three are choices you control. A return is set by the market, so it cannot be promised. These figures are invented for practice.

activities.title: Write the plan
activities.officeDescription: Bring the limit and the honest framing into one short plan.
activities.intro: You set a loss limit and separated a plan from a promise. Choose the written plan that keeps both.
activities.sourceIntro: A plan to file keeps the spare-only limit and makes no promise about the return.
activities.sourceExplanation: Each plan is one you could file. Only one keeps the limit and avoids promising a result. These are fictional examples.
activities.correctedHeadline: Invest the $20 spare, review in three months, sell at $10, and make no promise about the return.
activities.challengeTitle: Keep both the limit and the honesty.
activities.challengeText: One plan risks the whole $200 instead of the $20 spare. Another promises a $30 result no one can guarantee. The plan to file invests only the spare and makes no promise. These are fictional figures for practice.
activities.correctedFeedback: You filed the plan that keeps the loss limit and avoids a promised return. Both earlier lessons are in it.
activities.successFeedback: Your written plan risks only the $20 spare and promises nothing about the return. That is a plan you can keep.
activities.journalEvidence: The filed plan invested only the $20 spare, set a three-month review and a $10 sell point, and made no promise about the return. The rejected plans either risked the full $200 or promised a $30 result. These are fictional figures for practice.

choices.label: Keep the limit and the honesty
choices.detail: Invest only the $20 spare, review in three months, sell if it reaches $10, and state that returns are not guaranteed.

choices.label: Drop the limit
choices.detail: Invest the full $200 this month, review in three months, and state that returns are not guaranteed.

choices.label: Promise the gain
choices.detail: Invest the $20 spare and file that it will grow into $30.

evidence.title: The plan to file
evidence.explanation: This plan keeps the loss limit from the budget and the honesty from the earlier step. These figures are invented for practice.
